source: In the S bus, in the rush hour. A chap of about 26, felt hat with a cord instead of a ribbon, neck too long, as if someone’s been having a tug-of-war with it. People getting off. The chap in question gets annoyed with one of the men standing next to him. He accuses him of jostling him every time anyone goes past. A snivelling tone which is meant to be aggressive. When he sees a vacant seat he throws himself on to it. Two hours later, I meet him in the Cour de Rome, in front of the gare Saint-Lazare. He’s with a friend who’s saying: "You ought to get an extra button put on your overcoat." He shows him where (at the lapels) and why.

You are assisting with a scholarly experiment in structural literary analysis.

TASK: Write an ORIGINAL short prose passage in English, set in the target scenario below. It must be
a HOMEOSYNTACTIC transposition of a hidden source: hold the source's syntactic form at the level
specified below while inventing entirely new words and moving the content into the target
scenario. It is NOT a paraphrase or a translation.

FORM TARGET (hold this). Reproduce, period by period, the CLAUSE ARCHITECTURE below --- the same inventory and nesting of clauses (main / relative / adverbial / complement / coordinate, to the stated depth). The WORD ORDER and the words themselves are entirely yours; only the clause skeleton is fixed.
Reproduce it for all 10 periods, in this order:
Period 1 (~8 words) clause architecture: 1 main clause; subordination nested up to depth 0.
Period 2 (~29 words) clause architecture: 1 main clause; 1 open complement (infinitive); 1 adverbial clause; subordination nested up to depth 1.
Period 3 (~3 words) clause architecture: 1 main clause; subordination nested up to depth 0.
Period 4 (~15 words) clause architecture: 1 main clause; 1 relative/adnominal clause; subordination nested up to depth 1.
Period 5 (~11 words) clause architecture: 1 main clause; 1 adverbial clause; 1 relative/adnominal clause; subordination nested up to depth 2.
Period 6 (~9 words) clause architecture: 1 main clause; 1 relative/adnominal clause; 1 open complement (infinitive); subordination nested up to depth 2.
Period 7 (~12 words) clause architecture: 1 adverbial clause; 1 main clause; subordination nested up to depth 1.
Period 8 (~18 words) clause architecture: 1 main clause; subordination nested up to depth 0.
Period 9 (~19 words) clause architecture: 2 relative/adnominal clause; 1 main clause; 1 finite complement clause; 1 open complement (infinitive); subordination nested up to depth 4.

TARGET SCENARIO --- render the content here (in your own words):
  - an airport/border security checkpoint at a busy hour
  - the queue and the barriers; the divestment of belongings into trays
  - the scanners, metal detectors, and the body-search gesture
  - an officer and a traveller singled out of the line; documents and a wanded pat-down
  - the register of control: instructions, signage, the impersonal courtesy of authority

REQUIREMENTS --- both hold together:
1. CLAUSE ARCHITECTURE PRESERVED --- the same clause inventory and nesting depth per period, in any word order and words you choose.
2. COHERENT --- one continuous, fully sensible passage in the target scenario; new lexicon,
   no trace of any source content.

Write modern, natural English. Produce the 10 periods in order as continuous prose --- no
numbering, no headings. Output ONLY the passage: no preamble, no self-audit.

gens.text: The morning line stretched past the barriers. Travelers began to unburden their pockets, dropping keys and coins and phones into the gray trays, because the sign above the belt demanded it. The queue crept forward. An officer whose badge caught the light gestured toward a machine that hummed. Whenever the detector chimed, a passenger who had forgotten a belt stepped aside. She waved a wand, meaning to trace his outline. Because his boarding pass looked worn, the officer studied it closely. The scanner cast its blue arch over each shuffling shoulder and swallowed the endless procession whole. A man who had been singled out, whose documents the second officer now examined, understood that he must raise both arms and stand still. Everyone knew that the courtesy was only procedure.

The morning line coiled past the barriers. Travelers began to strip their pockets into gray trays, laying laptops flat and belts loose, while the conveyor pulled each bin forward under a hard blue light. The scanner hummed. A guard whose vest read SECURITY motioned the next passenger through the arch. When the alarm chimed, she pointed toward a mat that another officer guarded. She stepped aside, ordered to raise both arms. Because the wand demanded silence, no one in the queue spoke. His documents lay open on the steel counter beside the tray of surrendered coins and keys. The officer, who wore gloves that squeaked, announced that the pat-down was routine, a courtesy the signs promised, so she needed only to stand still. He said quietly that she was cleared.

The morning line coiled past the barriers. Travelers shuffled forward to empty their pockets into gray trays, unbuckling belts and surrendering laptops, while the conveyor swallowed each bag beneath a cold glare. The scanner hummed. A screen displayed the silhouette that every passing body briefly became. Because the machine flagged a shape that no one could quite name, an officer stepped closer. She raised a hand, gesturing him to spread his arms. When the wand traced his sleeve, the traveler stiffened. The overhead signage repeated its calm commands in three languages, courteous and utterly indifferent to the crowd. An officer whose gloves smelled faintly of latex, examining the passport that the man had offered, announced that the pat-down would take only a moment more. She said quietly that everything appeared to be in order.

The morning line coiled toward the barriers. Travelers were told to unpack their pockets, to surrender belts and coins into the gray trays, while a screen overhead flashed its silent, patient warnings. The queue crawled. A guard in a pale blue shirt watched the belt that fed each bag into the tunnel. Because the alarm chimed twice, a woman whose ticket trembled in her hand stepped aside. He asked her to raise both arms slightly. Once the wand had traced her sleeves, the officer nodded toward the far gate. Nobody protested, nobody hurried, and the courteous machinery of inspection absorbed the crowd without ever quite acknowledging a single face within it. A man who had forgotten his laptop, which lay orphaned in a tray behind him, discovered that the guard expected him to return and claim it. The sign insisted that all searches were routine.

The queue coiled toward the barriers. Travelers began to shed their coats and shoes into gray trays, though the belts kept jerking forward while the officer barked her patient, weary instructions above the din. Belongings slid onward. A single traveler, whom the scanner had flagged, stepped aside from the moving line. Because the machine chimed again, the man whose belt was studded halted where the tape marked. The officer signaled him to raise both arms. His documents lay open on the counter, and she wanded them down slowly. Once the pat-down finished, he gathered his scattered possessions from the trays. The signage overhead, which glowed in that impersonal blue, announced to every passenger who paused there that the checkpoint expected them to comply without complaint. The officer nodded that he could pass.

The line breathes forward in slow increments. To reach the barrier, each traveler must surrender the day's small architecture, so that keys and coins and belts descend into gray trays. The belt hums. Overhead a sign glows blue, whose pictograms instruct without ever quite explaining. Because the scanner blinks amber when a shape confuses it, the passenger whose bag it flagged is halted. A gesture waves her forward, a hand rising to indicate the frame. When the detector chimes, an officer steps out of stillness. She unfolds her documents onto the cold ledge, presenting them face-up, offering the impersonal proof of who she claims to be. The officer, whose wand traces the seams that a jacket hides, asks quietly that she raise her arms so he can finish. He nods, murmuring that she is free.

The queue folded back on itself twice. Travellers shuffled forward to empty their pockets, unbuckling belts and prying laptops from bags while a recorded voice repeated its instructions overhead. The trays advanced. A woman ahead of me placed her shoes in the bin that rolled toward the scanner. Because the alarm sounded when she stepped through the arch that framed the lane, an officer waved her aside. She was the traveller they chose to search more thoroughly. Once her documents lay flat on the counter, the officer raised his wand. He passed it slowly along her arms and down each leg with the practiced, impersonal courtesy of the uniformed. The man who watched her, and who wore the badge that marked his rank, murmured that she should turn so he could check the small of her back. He nodded and said that she was cleared.

The queue thickened toward the barriers. To reach the scanners the travellers shuffled forward slowly, though the officers kept waving them along whenever a tray came free. Belongings vanished. A woman ahead of me unlaced the boots that the signage demanded she remove. Because the detector chimed at a man whose belt still hung there, he stepped aside. He was singled out to prove that his pockets held nothing. When the wand swept his arms, the officer murmured a practiced apology. His documents lay open on the counter beside the empty trays. The traveller, whose passport an officer studied while the machine hummed on, seemed to understand that he would be released once the pat-down confirmed he carried only keys. I saw then that the courtesy meant nothing.

The morning queue coiled past the barriers. To reach the scanner, the traveller shuffled forward slowly, edging along the marked lane while the officers watched each passing tray with tired eyes. Belongings vanished. A laptop, which she had wrapped in a soft grey sleeve, slid into a bin. Because the belt jammed, the coat she had folded twice waited on the roller. A man was pulled aside to answer questions. When the wand approached, he lifted his arms. His documents lay open on the counter, his boarding pass creased at the corner, his passport thumbed to a stamped and crowded page. An agent who spoke in the flat courteous tone that signage everywhere seemed to echo announced that the search would take a moment more, asking him to stand still. She confirmed that everything read clear.

The line moves in slow, obedient increments. Everyone learns to empty their pockets into the gray trays before they step forward, because the officer at the arch will not repeat herself. Belts come off. A sign above the belt shows the coins and keys that travelers keep forgetting. When the machine beeps, a man whose bag has stalled on the rollers is asked to wait. He is chosen from the crowd, told to raise his arms. Because his boarding pass looks worn, an attendant studies it twice. The wand traces the seams of his jacket in short, impersonal sweeps that mean nothing personal. A woman who checks the screen and who nods at what the scanner reveals says the man may pass, and gestures for him to collect his tray. The signage insists that everyone comply.
